title: Bringing a PC Fallout 4 mod to Xbox or PlayStation through Creations (Bethesda.net): 2026 rules for size, archives and custom assets
content:
Bringing a PC Fallout 4 mod to Xbox or PlayStation through Creations (Bethesda.net): 2026 rules for size, archives and custom assets
Console mods are uploaded from the Creation Kit as Creations. The rules changed a lot in 2026 (from Bethesda's Fallout 4 patch notes):
- PlayStation can now take custom assets. Since the August 18, 2026 update, archives are supported on PlayStation and Creations may include .nif, .dds, .bink, .cdx, .csg, .wav and .fuz (with embedded .wav). Before that, PlayStation mods could only use assets already in the game, so older advice saying "no custom textures or meshes on PS4" is out of date.
- Xbox: Creations up to 2 GB can be uploaded (August 18, 2026).
- Storage for downloaded Creations (May 27, 2026): Xbox One up to 15 GB, Xbox Series X|S up to 100 GB, PlayStation 5 about 15 GB, PlayStation 4 about 16 GB (download size may not match space used).
- October 15, 2026 fixes: PC to PlayStation .nif conversion for filtered precombines, .ssf files allowed in archives, a PlayStation crash with Creations that add NPCs (FaceGen), and a temporary fix for crashes from looping .wav files (looping audio is only partly supported on PlayStation).
- Textures are stored differently per platform. The Creation Kit's Archive2 has separate texture archive formats for PC (DDS), Xbox (XBoxDDS) and PlayStation (GNF).
These rules keep changing: check the current Fallout 4 patch notes on help.bethesda.net before an upload.
Console memory is much tighter than a gaming PC's, so console versions of a mod usually ship 1K and 2K textures instead of 4K (see the texture memory entry).

title: How much memory Fallout 4 textures use at 4K, 2K and 1K (BC1, BC5, BC7) and what vanilla uses
content:
How much memory Fallout 4 textures use at 4K, 2K and 1K (BC1, BC5, BC7) and what vanilla uses
Block-compressed DDS sizes: BC1 (DXT1) uses half a byte per pixel; BC3 (DXT5), BC5 and BC7 use one byte per pixel. A full mipmap chain adds one third.
- 4K (4096): BC7/BC5/BC3 21.3 MB, BC1 10.7 MB
- 2K (2048): BC7/BC5/BC3 5.3 MB, BC1 2.7 MB
- 1K (1024): BC7/BC5/BC3 1.3 MB, BC1 0.7 MB
A diffuse + normal + specular set at 4K in BC7/BC5/BC5 is about 64 MB; at 2K about 16 MB; at 1K about 4 MB. Halving the size saves three quarters of the memory.
What the vanilla game uses (12,935 diffuse, 7,066 normal and 8,772 specular textures):
- Size of diffuse maps: 2048 for 49%, 1024 for 37%, 4096 for only 6%.
- Diffuse format: DXT1/BC1 67% (no alpha), DXT5/BC3 32% (with alpha), BC7 only 0.3%.
- Normal maps (_n): BC5 in 99.5%. Specular maps (_s): BC5 in 99%.
- In 6,334 complete diffuse/normal/specular sets, the normal map is the same size as the diffuse in 92% and larger in only 0.4%; the specular map is smaller than the diffuse in 17%.
- Mipmaps: 98.8% have a full mip chain. Always generate mipmaps; textures without them shimmer and waste bandwidth at a distance.

title: Making 1K and 2K textures look close to 4K (for console versions of a mod)
content:
Making 1K and 2K textures look close to 4K (for console versions of a mod)
A 1K texture has 1,048,576 pixels, a 4K about 16.8 million: one sixteenth of the information, and lost detail cannot be recovered. But what the player sees depends on more than resolution:
- Texel density matters more than resolution: pixels per metre of surface at normal viewing distance. Pack UVs tightly, mirror where nobody will notice, and give less space to hidden areas (undersides, backs, insides). Compare with vanilla density per category (see the texel density entry).
- Tile large surfaces instead of stretching one big unique texture. A BGSM material can tile without changing the mesh UVs: every BGSM has tile flags (bit 0 = U, bit 1 = V) followed by UV offset and UV scale values (U and V). Vanilla uses them, for example Stubble.BGSM at 3x and RabidFoam.BGSM at 10x. Trim sheets (strips of moulding, panels and edges on one texture) let many meshes share one sharp 1K map.
- Normal and specular maps carry much of the sense of detail. Use BC5 for both, as vanilla does. In the _s map, red is specular strength and green is gloss (see the specular map entry); real variation in the green channel makes a surface read as detailed. When cutting sizes, vanilla's habit is to shrink the specular first (smaller than the diffuse in 17% of vanilla sets), keep the normal the same size as the diffuse, and only rarely make the normal larger (0.4% of sets).
- Compression: BC7 keeps more detail than BC1 for diffuse maps but uses twice the memory of BC1 (the same as BC3). Vanilla diffuse maps are mostly BC1, or BC3 when they need alpha.
- Make the small version from the high-resolution source: downscale with a good filter (Lanczos or Kaiser, not a plain box filter), add a light sharpen, and generate full mipmaps. When converting PNG or TGA to DDS with texconv, use -srgb or the texture comes out darker.
- AI upscalers go the other way (1K to 4K with invented detail). That only helps a low-resolution source, not memory.
- Viewing distance sets the limit: first-person weapons, faces and anything seen up close look soft at 1K. Clutter, distant buildings and anything seen from a few metres away can look nearly the same as 4K at 1080p.
Practical rule: hero items close to the camera get 2K (4K only on PC), everything else a carefully unwrapped 1K with a good normal map, and large surfaces use tiling or trim sheets.

title: Fallout 4 specular map (_s) channels: red = specular strength, green = gloss (checked in the game's shaders)
content:
Fallout 4 specular map (_s) channels: red = specular strength, green = gloss (checked in the game's shaders)
Fallout 4's _s texture uses two channels:
- Red = specular strength: how bright the highlight is. White is shiny (metal, wet or polished surfaces), black has no highlight (cloth, dry dirt).
- Green = gloss (smoothness): how small and sharp the highlight is. White gives a tight, mirror-like highlight, black a broad, soft sheen.
- Blue and alpha are not read by the game.
How the game uses them (from the compiled shaders in Shaders011.fxp): the material shader samples only the red and green of the _s map. It writes green times the material's gloss value, and red times the material's specular value, into the lighting buffer; when a surface is wet, red is pushed towards 1. The lighting shader then turns gloss into a highlight power of 2^(10 x gloss + 1) (from 2 for gloss 0 up to 2048 for gloss 1) and multiplies the highlight by specular strength.
Save _s maps as BC5, like normal maps (99% of vanilla _s maps are BC5). BC5 stores exactly the red and green channels; the channels are not swapped by BC5 compression, despite some forum advice.
In Substance Painter or similar: put a specular or metal mask into red and smoothness (inverted roughness) into green. A flat grey _s with equal red and green makes everything look like the same plastic: give the green channel real variation (scratches, wet spots, worn edges) for surfaces to read as detailed.
tags: specular map _s red channel green channel gloss glossiness smoothness specular strength blue channel bc5 substance painter export shiny plastic look
verified_by: Disassembled all 3,939 shaders in the vanilla Textures\ShadersFX\Shaders011.fxp with D3DDisassemble (2026-11-05): the G-buffer shaders sample the _s slot as .xy and write G x material gloss and R (raised toward 1 when wet) x material specular; the deferred light shader uses that gloss as exp2(10*g + 1) with 1/(2*pi) normalisation and multiplies the highlight by the specular value. title: Good specular and gloss values for Fallout 4 _s maps per surface type (measured from vanilla)
content:
Good specular and gloss values for Fallout 4 _s maps per surface type (measured from vanilla)
Values from 0 to 1 (0 to 255 in an image editor); 10th percentile, typical (median) and 90th percentile of the vanilla game's _s maps, padding between UV islands excluded:
- Organic (plants, trees, fungus): specular 0.04 / 0.12 / 0.40, gloss 0.03 / 0.13 / 0.34
- Creatures (skin, flesh, fur): specular 0.04 / 0.21 / 0.41, gloss 0.05 / 0.22 / 0.58
- Rock and ground: specular 0.04 / 0.10 / 0.29, gloss 0.07 / 0.21 / 0.42
- Wood: specular 0.11 / 0.22 / 0.52, gloss 0.16 / 0.31 / 0.56
- Metal (weapons, machinery): specular 0.06 / 0.26 / 0.55, gloss 0.08 / 0.32 / 0.60
- Cloth: specular 0.08 / 0.25 / 0.51, gloss 0.06 / 0.19 / 0.57
Red is specular strength, green is gloss. Most vanilla surfaces are far less shiny than people expect: a typical plant is only about 0.12 specular and 0.13 gloss. Values near 1 everywhere make a surface look wet or like plastic.
For a real finish, let gloss vary: lower in crevices and on rough, detailed areas, higher on smooth raised parts, worn edges and wet spots. A flat grey _s with the same value in red and green is the most common cause of the "plastic" look.
The Mossy Blender add-on's Enhance Texture uses these ranges (Surface setting) when it builds an _s map.

title: texconv settings for Fallout 4 DDS: formats, mipmaps, sRGB and cutout leaves
content:
texconv settings for Fallout 4 DDS: formats, mipmaps, sRGB and cutout leaves
Settings that work for converting PNG to Fallout 4 DDS with texconv (the DirectXTex converter):
- Diffuse (_d): BC7_UNORM for best quality, or BC1 (no alpha) / BC3 (alpha) to match vanilla and save memory. Use -srgb, or texconv makes PNG colour darker.
- Normal (_n) and specular (_s): BC5_UNORM. Converting a test gradient to BC5 kept the values with no flag, with -srgb and with --ignore-srgb; --ignore-srgb is the safe choice for data maps so mipmaps are filtered on the raw values.
- Mipmaps: -m 0 makes the full chain (98.8% of vanilla textures have one). -if CUBIC filters them better than the default box filter; texconv has no Kaiser filter (NVIDIA Texture Tools does).
- Cutout textures (leaves, grass, fences with alpha test): --keep-coverage 0.5 keeps the alpha edges from thinning out or vanishing in the smaller mipmaps (vanilla alpha test threshold is 127, about 0.5).
- -bc x gives the best (slowest) BC7 compression.
Example for a leaf diffuse: texconv -f BC7_UNORM -m 0 -if CUBIC -srgb --keep-coverage 0.5 -bc x -o out leaf_d.png
Example for a normal map: texconv -f BC5_UNORM -m 0 -if CUBIC --ignore-srgb -o out leaf_n.png

title: Mossy Blender add-on Texture Helpers: upscaling and enhancing a texture that is only inside Blender
content:
Mossy Blender add-on Texture Helpers: upscaling and enhancing a texture that is only inside Blender
Since add-on 5.4.9 the Texture Helpers buttons (Fallout 4 > Texture Helpers) work on the texture on the active mesh, even when it was never saved to disk (baked, packed or AI-generated):
- Upscale Texture on Object: AI upscale (Real-ESRGAN) one texture 2x or 4x. The result is packed into the .blend and plugged into the same material slot; the old image stays in the file. "Also Save To" writes a copy to a folder.
- Upscale All Object Textures: every map at once. Colour maps use the AI; normal and other data maps get a clean resize (normals renormalised), because a photo-trained AI damages their values.
- Enhance Texture on Object: AI-upscales the colour map 4x, then builds from that detail: a normal map laid over the mesh's existing normal map (the baked shape is kept), and an _s map with red = specular and green = gloss in the vanilla range for the chosen Surface (Organic, Creature, Rock/Ground, Wood, Metal, Cloth). Output size: same, 2x or 4x. Optional DDS (BC7 / BC5 / BC5, full mipmaps).
- The small folder button next to each works on a file instead.
If the AI upscaler cannot run, the add-on uses a plain resize and says "NOT AI" in its message.
Error "_wfopen ...models/realesrgan-x4plus.param failed" (or every upscale looks like a plain resize): Real-ESRGAN's NCNN program only loads models from a folder whose path contains "models". Older add-on installs moved the model files out of that folder. Add-on 5.4.9 repairs it automatically; by hand, put realesrgan-x4plus.param and .bin into a "models" folder next to realesrgan-ncnn-vulkan.exe.

title: Making a mesh's texture photo-realistic in a chosen style with local AI (ComfyUI) without breaking the UVs
content:
Making a mesh's texture photo-realistic in a chosen style with local AI (ComfyUI) without breaking the UVs
What works, tested on an AI-generated flower (7,400 triangles, 407 UV islands), all local:
1. Render the mesh from many angles in Blender with plain colour (emission, no lighting), for example 21 views: 8 around at low height, 4 higher, 1 from the top, 4 from below and 4 at mid height. Save the camera of each view.
2. Repaint each view in ComfyUI with a photo-real SDXL model (RealVisXL) at about 0.85 denoise, guided by ControlNet Union SDXL with TWO guides: depth (strength 1.0) and canny edges of the render (about 0.9). Without them the AI either keeps the shape and stays painterly (0.5 denoise) or turns photo-real but paints a different plant (0.65).
3. Show the AI the target style with IP-Adapter (style transfer, weight about 0.6) using crops of your own reference textures, plus a prompt describing the material.
4. Project every repainted view back onto the UV texture. Each texel takes its colour from the views that see it most head-on (not near a silhouette or depth edge, and not hidden behind other parts). Texels no view sees take the colour of the nearest painted texel, not the old texture.
Results: 98% of the texture was seen by at least one of 21 views, 91% painted fully from the views; the projection matched the renders with 99.8% overlap.
What does not work: running img2img directly on the UV texture. With hundreds of islands the AI sees abstract shapes, not a flower.
Needed downloads (free, licences checked): ControlNet Union SDXL promax (Apache-2.0), IP-Adapter Plus SDXL ViT-H and CLIP-ViT-H image encoder (Apache-2.0), ComfyUI_IPAdapter_plus node (GPL-3.0).

title: Fallout 4 material (BGSM/BGEM) and shader rules from the whole game: what each feature needs, NIF flags vs the material file, plant materials, glow vs greyscale slot
content:
Fallout 4 material (BGSM/BGEM) and shader rules from the whole game: what each feature needs, NIF flags vs the material file, plant materials, glow vs greyscale slot
Scan of the unpacked game (9,024 material files: 8,336 BGSM + 688 BGEM, 136,789 mesh shapes in 42,605 NIFs). Counts are vanilla.
The NIF's shader flags copy the BGSM exactly: Tree/Tree_Anim, two-sided, glow map, environment mapping, hair, decal, cast shadows, z-write, greyscale-to-palette, skin tint, anisotropic lighting, external emittance all agree on every vanilla shape (for example two-sided 9,942 shapes, 0 differ). Alpha test is the exception: it is set in the BGSM and the NIF's NiAlphaProperty, not in the shader flags (8,530 shapes use BGSM alpha with no NiAlphaProperty). Keep the NIF and its BGSM in agreement.
What features come with: glow map always has a glow (_g) texture (272 of 272; an empty glow slot has crashed the game on cell load); greyscale-to-palette colour always has a greyscale palette texture (478 of 478) and that slot is the PALETTE, not the glow map (vanilla never puts a _g there, 0 of 272); reflections (environment mapping) name a cube map in 3,001 of 3,030 and a specular map in 2,990; back lighting comes with two-sided + alpha test (52 of 53); skin tint with subsurface lighting (27 of 27); wind (tree) materials are alpha-tested (91 of 93) and never use reflections (0 of 93).
Alpha test reference: 127/128 most, 90 for hair, about 100 for grass; 255 hides the mesh (only Bethesda's 'turned off' materials use it).
Plant/grass/tree materials (175 under Materials\Landscape\Plants, Grass, Trees): two-sided 82%, alpha test 91% (ref 127), subsurface 61% (rolloff 0.3 most common), back lighting only 25% (power 0.2-0.4 when on), rim lighting 0, non-occluder 69% of plants. Lighting shader types: Default 82,354, Environment_Map 29,827, Glow 3,874, Hair_Tint 1,945 (90% vertex colours), Skin_Tint 1,872, Face_Tint 1,627; 14,931 effect-shader shapes (1,604 with a .bgem).
Mossy Blender add-on: Check Against Game (Export panels) compares a mesh's materials and textures with these rules and prints every finding with its vanilla count; the same check runs after each NIF export. Re-exporting an imported game mesh now starts from the game's own BGSM (subsurface, non-occluder and similar fields survive). Glow textures go only to the glow slot. Foliage materials get the vanilla plant settings (no forced rim/back lighting).

title: Which DDS format and size Fallout 4 uses for each texture (diffuse _d, normal _n, specular _s, glow _g, palette, cube map _e, mask _m) and how the game's cube maps are used
content:
Which DDS format and size Fallout 4 uses for each texture (diffuse _d, normal _n, specular _s, glow _g, palette, cube map _e, mask _m) and how the game's cube maps are used
From the 22,266 textures vanilla materials reference (DDS headers read):
- Diffuse (_d): BC1 (no alpha) or BC3 (with alpha) - 6,564 of 6,566 in BGSMs; mostly 2048, then 1024 and 4096.
- Normal (_n): BC5 (4,714 of 4,725). The game reads only red and green of a normal map.
- Specular/smoothness (_s): BC5 (4,729 of 4,752): red = specular, green = smoothness.
- Glow (_g): BC1 (158 of 176).
- Greyscale palette: small uncompressed RGBA, 16-256 px (84 of 96 uncompressed).
- Cube map (_e): a real cube map (96-100%), uncompressed 128 px per side or BC1 32 px.
- Reflection mask (_m): BC1.
Almost every texture has a full mip chain (99%) and power-of-two sides; textures without mips shimmer and cost more at a distance (only a few interface notes lack them).
Cube maps: the game has 72 under Textures\Shared\Cubemaps, almost all 128 px per side (512 KB). One of them, mipblur_DefaultOutside1.dds, is used by about 60% of all reflective shapes (19,110 shapes plus 1,932 materials); the 'mipblur' ones have pre-blurred mip levels, and smoothness picks the mip (rougher = blurrier).

title: How Fallout 4 particle effects (fire, smoke, sparks, steam, blood, dust, water) are built in the NIF: modifiers, flipbooks, blend modes, soft particles, and vanilla values to copy
content:
How Fallout 4 particle effects (fire, smoke, sparks, steam, blood, dust, water) are built in the NIF: modifiers, flipbooks, blend modes, soft particles, and vanilla values to copy
Every vanilla particle effect is a NiParticleSystem inside a NIF (745 NIFs, 1,681 systems; most under Meshes\Effects). Every system has NiPSysData (bs_max_vertices = max particles), an emitter (box 746, mesh 482, sphere 272, cylinder 181), NiPSysAgeDeathModifier, NiPSysSpawnModifier, NiPSysPositionModifier, NiPSysBoundUpdateModifier, BSPSysLODModifier (fade by distance) and BSPSysSimpleColorModifier (fade in/out + 3 colour keys over life); most also BSPSysScaleModifier (size over life, 1,597), NiPSysGravityModifier (with turbulence), NiPSysDragModifier and NiPSysRotationModifier. The birth rate is the NiPSysEmitterCtlr's float interpolator. The look comes from a BSEffectShaderProperty (texture, soft-particle depth, palette, falloff) plus the NiAlphaProperty blend mode.
Animated (flipbook) textures: BSPSysSubTexModifier (520 uses) plays frames stored as NiPSysData subtexture offsets, each rectangle (u0, width, v0, height): SmokeBurstPuffAnim is 8x8 = 64 frames, FireballLoop_anim 8x4 = 32, FireTorchFlameAnim 16x8 = 128.
Vanilla recipes (median per kind): fire - additive blend (SrcAlpha/One), life 0.6 s, 30 per second, start size 20, flipbook 32 frames about 43 fps, soft particles 81%; smoke - normal alpha blend (SrcAlpha/InvSrcAlpha), life 2 s, 15 per second, start size about 38, soft particles 88% (depth about 40), greyscale palette 69%, gravity 71%; sparks - additive, life 0.4 s, tiny (size 1, 64 px texture), gravity 87%; steam - flipbook 64 frames, life 2.5 s, soft 85%; blood - alpha blend, palette 100%, soft depth 5; dust - alpha blend, life 1 s; energy - additive, soft 100%. All 101 vanilla particle textures are DXT5 (BC3), mostly 512-1024 px, so a 64-frame flipbook has only about 128 px per frame - why vanilla fire and smoke look soft close up.
Tools: PyNifly does not read particle blocks; NifSkope and the Niftools reader (nifgen) do.

title: How Fallout 4 reflections (cube maps / environment maps) work, which cube map most of the game uses, and how to make HD cube maps without seams
content:
How Fallout 4 reflections (cube maps / environment maps) work, which cube map most of the game uses, and how to make HD cube maps without seams
Reflective materials (environment mapping on, 3,030 vanilla BGSMs) name a cube map, almost always under Textures\Shared\Cubemaps. The game has 72: 46 are 128 px per side, uncompressed BGRA8 with 8 mips (512 KB); 26 are 32 px BC1/BC3 (old ore/gem ones). mipblur_DefaultOutside1.dds, a capture of a Commonwealth street with sky and ground, is used by about 60% of all reflective shapes; its _dielectric, _bronze and _Copper versions and mipblur_InstInterior cover most of the rest.
How the game picks the blur: 202 of 205 cube map lookups in the game's pixel shaders use a plain sample, so the graphics card picks the mip level from how fast the reflection direction changes across the screen (bumpy or curved surfaces read lower, blurrier mips; flat smooth ones read the top level). Smoothness does not pick the mip. The 'mipblur' maps are pre-blurred: each lower mip keeps only about 40% of the detail a plain downsample would.
Making HD cube maps that fit: keep the same file name and path (a loose file in a mod replaces the game's), make every side the same power of two (512), give it a full mip chain, and blur each lower mip the way the vanilla map does at that same size, or rough metal turns mirror-like. Upscaling the six sides separately makes visible seams (the step across an edge was 3-5 times a normal pixel step); upscale each side with a border taken from its neighbours, blend the borders, and weld the edge texels so both sides match - then the seams are smoother than vanilla's own (about 0.6 of a pixel step at the worst edge).
tags: cube map cubemap reflection environment map envmap _e mipblur_DefaultOutside1 shared cubemaps HD cube map seams mips blur shiny metal chrome reflection quality

title: Fallout 4 effect records in the plugins: effect shaders (EFSH), explosions (EXPL), impacts (IPCT/IPDS), projectiles (PROJ), lights (LIGH), art objects (ARTO), hazards (HAZD)
content:
Fallout 4 effect records in the plugins: effect shaders (EFSH), explosions (EXPL), impacts (IPCT/IPDS), projectiles (PROJ), lights (LIGH), art objects (ARTO), hazards (HAZD)
The official plugins (Fallout4.esm + 6 DLCs) hold 70 effect shaders, 342 explosions, 865 impacts in 371 impact data sets, 239 projectiles, 1,065 lights, 258 art objects and 78 hazards.
- EFSH (effect shader, the glow/membrane on actors and objects): fill texture (67 of 70), membrane palette (56), blend Source Alpha/One (additive, 39) or Source Alpha/Inverted Alpha (28); 65 have 'No Particle Shader' (FO4 does particles in NIFs, not here); greyscale palette flags common. The data layout changed at form version 106 (3 old records keep the old one).
- EXPL: a model (336 of 342 have one: the NIF with the particle effect), light, sounds, impact data set, radius (median outer radius 200), force, damage, image space modifier.
- PROJ: type Missile 117, Lobber 52, Beam 52, Arrow 7, Flame 6, Cone 5; median speed 1,400; links to light, muzzle flash light and model, explosion.
- IPCT: impact NIF, duration, orientation (Surface Normal 461, Projectile Reflection 392), decal size, texture set; IPDS maps each material type to an impact.
- LIGH: radius (median 256), colour, falloff, FOV, flicker (257 lights) or pulse (49), shadow type (spot 113, omni 87), non-specular 166.
So a full effect = record (EXPL/PROJ/IPCT/EFSH) -> NIF with particle systems -> effect textures/BGEM; changing the look usually means the NIF and its textures, the timing/size means the record.

title: Bringing an old Fallout 4 texture mod up to date: what to check and how to batch-upscale it without damaging it
content:
Bringing an old Fallout 4 texture mod up to date: what to check and how to batch-upscale it without damaging it
Audit first (read only), comparing every DDS with the same file in the current game:
- Resolution: an older retexture can now be SMALLER than the game's own file (2,076 of 10,866 in one 2021 mod, mostly 1024 where the game has 2048), so the mod makes things blurrier than vanilla. Check whether those are real art changes before deleting them (56 of 60 sampled were).
- Format: vanilla normal and specular maps are BC5 (in the unpacked game plus DLC: 7,022 of 7,066 _n and 8,709 of 8,772 _s); old mods often use BC3/DXT5 or BC7. Check that normal maps are not channel-swapped.
- Alpha: BC1 keeps 1-bit cut-out alpha, so a BC1 texture whose vanilla file is BC3 is usually fine; compare the actual alpha. Lower alpha on a blended glass texture can be intended (moss on glass).
- Terrain LOD textures and .btr/.bto files are generated for one load order and game version: regenerate them with xLODGen (run through Mod Organizer) instead of editing them.
Upscaling rules that held up when measured: AI upscalers (Real-ESRGAN) are good for colour maps but shift their average colour (about 3/255 darker in 36 of 40), so match each channel's average back to the original. Do NOT AI-upscale normal maps (directions turned about 7 degrees on average) or specular maps (the fine grain is smoothed away, one map lost 35% of its shine): resize those exactly (Lanczos), keep red and green as resized and rebuild blue from them, then save colour maps as BC7 with full mipmaps. Specular maps: save as BC5 with NO alpha, like vanilla (see the ENB section below: a specular alpha is what makes ENB parallax smear). Normal maps: BC5 like vanilla. Output to a separate mod placed below the original.
Measuring trap: Texconv's resize weights colour by alpha, so comparing a texture that has alpha after shrinking it with Texconv shows false differences; decode at full size and shrink each channel separately.
Better normal and specular maps after an AI upscale: in that mod the normal maps had been generated from the colour maps (their X/Y followed the colour map's slopes, correlation 0.5-0.8) and the specular maps too (correlation 0.58-0.92). So they can be rebuilt: take the fine detail the AI added to the colour map (AI colour minus a plain resize, high-passed), turn it into slopes at the strength the original normal map shows, measure the X/Y sign per texture (some maps use the opposite convention), and add it to the exactly-resized original normal, keeping the alpha. For specular, add the same detail per channel at the strength measured on the original, only where the relation is clear. Result: same shapes (correlation 0.98-1.00), more fine relief, averages within 3/255, parallax alpha unchanged.
ENB Complex Parallax in Fallout 4 reads its height map from the ALPHA channel of the SPECULAR (_s) map: 255 = no parallax, darker = pushed down. Surfaces that look stretched or smeared toward the camera with ENB parallax on usually have something else in that alpha. In one older moss texture mod, 350 of 952 specular maps had a copy of the diffuse cut-out mask there (plants, decals, puddles, road overlays, stains, mossy rocks and bark), so ENB read the mask as deep holes. Setting only the mask-like alphas to 255 did NOT fix it in game (see the most reliable fix below). Telling a real height map from a soft-edged mask by its numbers is also unreliable: in the same mod 153 of 952 alphas were soft or gradient rather than hard 0/255 masks, and removing all of them is what stopped the smearing.
Height scale for ENB Complex Parallax (Fallout 4): 255 = parallax off, 127 = the surface (no shift), darker = pushed in, brighter = pushed out. To give a flat texture real depth, make a height map (best: integrate the normal map so the depth matches the lighting) and write it as 127 for the top of the relief down to about 50-90 for crevices; keep cut-out areas at 127, not 255, so the edges do not switch between on and off. Raised values (above 127) and masks smear. Install a specular fix as its own mod BELOW the original texture mod in Mod Organizer or it does not win. Known issue: ENB 0.501 on next-gen Fallout 4 (1.10.98x/1.11.x) has user reports of smearing on rocks and rubble even with correct heights; test a few textures before converting a whole mod.
Most reliable fix for ENB parallax smearing from a texture mod's specular maps: remove the alpha channel entirely and save the specular maps as BC5 like vanilla (red = specular, green = smoothness). Setting the alpha to 255 in a compressed format such as BC7 is not reliable: compression left values of 251-254 in a test, and ENB treats anything below exactly 255 as parallax on (above 127 = raised), so the smearing stayed. With no alpha the shader reads 1.0 = off on every pixel.
Mossy can do this for you: Textures & Materials > ENB Specular Fix. Pick one mod folder, or the Mod Organizer mods folder with 'Every mod inside this folder'. Scan lists every specular map that is not BC5; Fix re-saves them as BC5 with no alpha (red and green kept), also from texture BA2 archives (needs BSArch, which comes with xEdit), and writes the copies to a new folder '<mod> - ENB Specular Fix' next to the mod; the original mod is never changed. Enable that folder in Mod Organizer BELOW its mod. Do not run it on a mod that was made for ENB Complex Parallax on purpose (its description says so): it removes that mod's parallax too. Tested on the original 2021 texture archive (3.9 GB): 952 of 952 specular maps converted in about 2 minutes, every output BC5 at the same size, shine and smoothness changed by about 1/255.
